# Conductor

> Run graphs of typed Python functions.

Conductor runs graphs of nodes. A node is a plain Python function, and its typed signature is its interface: its parameters are its inputs, and its return type says what its outputs are.

A graph is data, called a graph record. It lists the nodes, what each node's inputs get (a constant, a graph input, or edges from other nodes' outputs), and the graph's own outputs. `Graph.compile(record, registry)` turns a record into a `Graph`. It reports what is wrong with the graph instead of raising.

A `Graph` runs. A node wired to a series, a list that a node returns as `Series[T]`, is called once per item. A run is one value, a `Run`. It can pause to ask a person, go on later, and write itself as JSON.

The host is the application that uses conductor. It declares its own types and nodes.

## Quick Start

One node returns many values, one takes a single value, and one takes them all. That is all there is to iteration.

```python
registry = NodeRegistry()


@registry.node("lines", title="Lines", description="The lines of a text.")
def lines(text: str) -> Series[str]:
    return text.splitlines()


@registry.node("upper", title="Uppercase", description="Turns a text into capital letters.")
def upper(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper()


@registry.node("join", title="Join", description="Joins every text it is given.")
def join(texts: Series[str]) -> str:
    """Joins every text it is given."""
    return "+".join(texts)


assert upper("a") == "A"  # a node is called like its function

graph = Graph.compile(GraphRecord.model_validate({            # a graph is data: a GraphRecord, or its JSON text
    "nodes": {
        "lines": {"node": "lines", "inputs": {"text": {"graph_input": "text"}}},
        "upper": {"node": "upper", "inputs": {"text": {"sources": [{"node": "lines", "output": "result"}]}}},
        "join": {"node": "join", "inputs": {"texts": {"sources": [{"node": "upper", "output": "result"}]}}},
    },
    "outputs": {"result": {"node": "join", "output": "result"}},
}), registry)
assert graph.is_runnable, graph.problems

run = graph.run(text="a\nb\nc")    # the graph input text, declared on lines
run.outputs                        # {"result": "A+B+C"}: what the graph returns, by the names its outputs declare
run.results["upper"]["result"]     # ["A", "B", "C"]: ran once per item of lines.result
run.results["join"]["result"]      # "A+B+C": Series[str] received every value, once
```

The same graph is shorter written with `make_graph(lines, upper, join)`, which "Writing a graph in Python" explains.

## Core Concepts

### The Node Contract

A node is a function under `@node`. Its signature says its inputs and outputs, and the decorator says the rest:

`@node("id", version=, title=, description=, category=, tags=, extra=, docs=, asks=, policy=, deprecation=, compute_added_inputs=, compute_outputs=, replaces=, upgrade=)`

- `@node(...)` wraps a plain function and returns a `FunctionDefinition`. The definition is frozen and can be called like the function. It registers nothing.
- `@registry.node(...)` takes the same arguments, and also adds the node to that registry.
- `subgraph("id", title=, description=, ...)(record)` makes a `SubgraphDefinition`, a node made of a graph record. It has no function, so calling it is a type error.
- `NodeDefinition` is the union of the two. Code that reads a definition tells them apart with `match`.

The id, `title` and `description` are required. The title and description are what a person reads about the node. The docstring is for the developer and is never shown. So an empty `title` or `description`, or one of only spaces, raises a `NodeDeclarationError` of `empty_title_or_description`.

A field's title is what its `Param(title=)` says, and `None` without one. Nothing is guessed from the field's name. A host that shows a label for an untitled field writes its own from `name`.

`extra` is the host's own JSON about the node. Conductor keeps it and describes it, but never reads it.

`category` is the group a palette lists the node under, and `""` when it has none. The host decides what the groups are. A definition has it as `definition.category`, and a registry can give its nodes one (see "conductor").

**Inputs.** An input is a parameter, such as `text: str`. To say more about it, wrap its type in `Annotated` with a `Param`: `Annotated[str, Param(title=, description=, widget=, constant_only=, ge=, le=, max_length=, ...)]`.

- A widget is optional. Without one, the host's editor picks a control from the input's type, such as a line of text for a `str`. Give an input a widget only when the editor should show more than its type says, such as a `Textarea` for a long text.
- A default makes an input optional. The default is checked against the type, and written as JSON once, where it is declared. A default that isn't of the input's type, or that the type can't write as JSON, is `default_invalid`.
- A limit that can't apply to the type, such as `ge` on a `str`, is refused where it is written (`limit_not_supported`).
- `Param`s can be stacked. An alias such as `Annotated[str, Param(widget=TextInput())]` can be wrapped again with `Param(min_length=1)`. They merge the way pydantic merges stacked fields: for each argument and each limit, the later `Param` wins wherever it isn't `None`. So a later `constant_only=False` turns an earlier `True` off, and a later `title=None` leaves the title as it was.
- A `Param` on the item of a `Series` is the field's.

**Constant only.** Some inputs are settings, fixed when the graph is drawn. `Param(constant_only=True)` says that an input takes only a constant: the record's, or its own default. It never takes an edge or a graph input. Every input whose value a hook reads takes only a constant too, with no `Param` needed. A hook parameter annotated `type` reads only the type arriving on the input's edge, so that input can still be wired.

- Its `FieldDescription` has `constant_only` true, so an editor offers it no edge.
- `make_graph` never wires it, or makes it a graph input, by itself.
- Compiling a record that gives it `sources` or a `graph_input` is `input_takes_only_a_constant`, and `ctx.given` says which of the two.
- With no constant and no default, it is `input_has_no_value`, variant `constant_only`.
- `constant_only` on an output is `constant_only_on_output`.

**Choices.** `Param(choices=[...])` is the one place a field's choices are declared. Each choice is a value, or a `Choice(id, title)` from `conductor` to give it a title. A `Choice` carries any other keyword it is given along with it: `Choice("ida", "Ida B.", team="sales")`. The field's record has the choices as `choices`, a tuple of `Choice`.

- On a `Literal` field, the choices give its values titles, one each. On any other field, they limit what it takes.
- Each choice is read the way an answer is: strictly, from its JSON form, and held to the field's limits. So an enum's value, or a date's ISO text, can be a choice.
- A value is one of the choices when its JSON is. A dict's keys may come in any order, and a float that isn't finite is written as its text. This holds for an input, a return and an answer alike.
- A value is compared in the JSON form its type reads it into. So `1` picks a `float` choice `1.0`. But on `Annotated[Any, Param(choices=[1])]`, `True` and `1.0` are refused.
- `{"a": 1, "b": 2}` and `{"b": 2, "a": 1}`, given as choices, are one choice given twice.
- `None` is never a pick. A type that takes `None` takes it beside its choices. That goes for an answer and an `Ask`'s default too.
- A value outside the choices is refused with "the value is not one of the choices". That is the problem of wherever the value came in (`invalid_input`, `invalid_value`, `invalid_output` or `invalid_answer`), with `not_a_choice` in its `errors`.
- A `Series` answer that picks one choice twice is refused with "a choice is picked twice" (`picked_twice` in its `errors`). Only an answer must pick each choice once, so a node may return a `Series` that has a value twice.
- Without `choices`, a `Literal` field's choices are its values. That includes `None` when the `Literal` lists it, as `Literal["a", None]` does; `Literal["a"] | None` takes `None` beside its one choice.
- With `choices`, `None` is not one of them. So `Annotated[Literal["a", None], Param(choices=["a"])]` takes `"a"`, and takes `None` beside it.
- An `Ask` can give a question choices that only the run knows. Otherwise a question has its output's choices.
- Choices that can't be used are `choices_invalid`.

**Outputs.** The return type declares the outputs.

- `-> str` is one output, named `result`. `Annotated[str, Param(title=)]` says more about it.
- A frozen dataclass is one output per field. The class is the definition's `outputs_dataclass`, which is `None` for any other return type.
- Any other type is one value, a `dict[str, int]` included.
- With `compute_outputs`, the function returns the outputs the hook gives, as a mapping by name.
- `-> None` declares no outputs.

**Branches.** A node can choose which of its outputs gets a value. `Param(exclusive_group=)` on the fields of a returned dataclass makes them alternatives, called branches. Exactly one of them has a value on each call; anything else is `invalid_output`.

- `return SKIPPED` chooses none, and skips every output.
- A node that may choose none in a group, while giving its other outputs values, makes "none" a branch of its own: `neither: Annotated[bool, Param(exclusive_group="size")]`.
- A branch's default is `SKIPPED`, or it has none. Any other default is `default_invalid`.

**`None`.** A value can be `None`.

- An input gets `None` only if its type says so, as `email: str | None` or `Any` do. Otherwise the node isn't called for that item. Its outputs are `None` there, and `run.not_called` records the node, the item and the input.
- Of its branches (the outputs of an `exclusive_group`, or those whose default is `SKIPPED`), none is chosen there. So what is wired to any branch is skipped there.
- `Series[X]` leaves `None` items out, and `Series[X | None]` keeps them (see "One or many").
- `Series[X] | None` is a list, or `None` in its place. `Table[R] | None` is a table, or `None`. Such an input takes `None` given as a constant or as its default. A node may return `None` for either. And a list or table that was never returned (its node had a `None` argument, or returned `None`) reaches it as `None`.
- `Series[X] = None`, without `| None`, is `default_invalid`.

**A skip wins.** A node with one input on a branch not chosen, and another input that is `None`, is skipped, whatever the order of its parameters.

- A skip also wins over an input whose edge names a field its record lacks. That input fails the call (`invalid_edge_value`, for the first such input in the signature) only when no input is skipped.
- A skip wins over an input with no value yet, too. The node is skipped at once, and the nodes downstream go on while the other input's source still waits for a person.

**Skipping and asking.** The function returns `SKIPPED` on a branch not chosen. It raises `Ask(...)` when a person must answer, and its `@node` says so with `asks=True`. `Ask` is a `BaseException`, so an `except Exception` in the node lets it through. "Asking a person" has the rules.

**The run's context.** What the host supplies for a run reaches a node as its first parameter, typed `Context[X]`. "Context" has the rules.

**What `@node` checks.** These raise a `NodeDeclarationError`, whose one problem in `problems` has the code as its `type`:

- an `async def`;
- a parameter with no type;
- `*args`, or `**kwargs` with no `compute_added_inputs`;
- a dataclass of outputs that isn't frozen;
- a field name that is gone from the next version, with no `Upgrade`;
- an `Upgrade` rename from or to a field its version doesn't declare.

### Versions and Policies

A node can have several versions. Each version is a `@node` with the same id, and it names the version before it in `replaces=`. The decorated function is the newest.

- A definition is one version. The older versions are plain `@node` definitions that are never registered. Only the newest goes on a registry.
- An id the registry already has is `duplicate_node_id`, whatever `replaces=` names. `registry.replace(newer)` swaps a node the registry has.
- `definition.versions` is the node at each of its versions: a read-only mapping by version number, newest first.

```python
@node("greet", title="Greet", description="Greets a person by name.")
def greet_v1(name: Annotated[str, Param(title="Name", widget=Textarea())]) -> str:
    return f"Hello {name}"

def _split_name(values: dict) -> dict:
    first, _, last = values.pop("name").partition(" ")
    return {**values, "first": first, "last": last}

@node("greet", title="Greet", description="Greets a person by first and last name.", policy=Policy(retries=2, retry_delay=0.5, attempt_timeout=10, concurrency=4), replaces=greet_v1, upgrade=Upgrade(rewrite=_split_name))
def greet(first: str, last: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello {first} {last}"

assert list(greet.versions) == [2, 1] and greet.versions[1] is greet_v1
```

**Policy.** A node's `Policy` says how it is called: `Policy(concurrency=None, retries=0, retry_delay=1.0, attempt_timeout=None, retry_on=(), reuse_when_inputs_match=True, costs_nothing=False)`. Retries are in "Retries and Timeouts", `reuse_when_inputs_match` in "Running again", and `costs_nothing` under "Running".

`concurrency` limits how many calls of the node run at once.

- With `concurrency=None`, the default, each place a graph uses the node is called one item at a time. It takes no notice of other places or other runs. So two runs at once in one process can call it at the same time, and so can two places in one run when the node is called on threads.
- With `concurrency=n`, at most `n` calls of the node run at once in the whole process. That counts every place a graph uses the node, and every run going on. That is how a node keeps to an outside service's quota.
- For example, take `concurrency=2`, and two runs at once that each use `fetch` in two places. Together they make two calls of `fetch` at once. The other calls wait, while each run calls its other nodes.
- When a call ends, the waiting runs ask again, and the first to ask starts. A run that just made a call gives the others a moment first, so one busy run can't keep the others out. A free place is never kept for a run that isn't asking.
- What counts together is one definition, what one `@node` made. A registry's copy of it, with the registry's tags, counts with it. A node declared again under the same id counts apart.
- A call counts until its function returns. So a call given up at its `attempt_timeout` still counts while its thread runs. A call waiting to be retried doesn't count.
- Watch out for nesting. Say a node's function runs a graph that uses the node again, or uses a node that uses it back. Then `concurrency` deadlocks once the nesting is as deep as `concurrency`: the outer calls hold every place, and the inner run waits for one.
- With `concurrency` 1 or `None` and no `attempt_timeout`, the node is called in order on the run's own thread. Otherwise it is called on threads.

The values are checked. `concurrency` is at least 1, or `None`. `retries` is at least 0. `retry_delay` is a finite number of seconds, at least 0, and `attempt_timeout` a finite number of seconds above 0. `Policy` is a frozen pydantic dataclass read strictly, so anything else raises pydantic's own validation error. A yes or no, a text, or `1.5` is not a whole number.

**Version numbers and upgrades.**

- `version=` is one past the version replaced, or 1, unless the node gives its own number. A number given must be above the version replaced (`version_not_after`). A host whose subgraphs have their own numbers gives them this way.
- `Upgrade(renamed_inputs={old: new}, renamed_outputs={old: new}, rewrite=fn)` goes beside `replaces=`. It says how a graph record moves to the new version.
  - An input rename carries the input's entry along: its constant, its graph input or the edges into it.
  - An output rename carries the edges out of the output, those out of a field of it, and the graph outputs that name it.
  - `fn` takes the node's constants and graph-input defaults as one dict, and returns them. A default stays a default, and every other key it returns is written as a constant. A value for an input that edges lead into is refused (`invalid_record`).
  - An input the new version neither keeps nor renames loses what it gets: its constant, its graph input or the edges into it. `fn` sees its constant or default first. Since every key `fn` returns is written, `fn` leaves out the keys of inputs that are gone, as `_split_name` above pops `name`. A key it keeps for a gone input is `unknown_input` when the graph is compiled.
  - A subgraph's inputs are the graph inputs its record names.
  - An `Upgrade` is required only when a field name of the replaced version is gone, for a subgraph as for a function. A gone input needs a rename or `fn`, and a gone output a rename. Without one, the declaration raises `upgrade_missing`.
  - Each rename starts at a field the replaced version declares and ends at one the new version declares, or the declaration raises `upgrade_renames_unknown`. A version with a `compute_added_inputs` hook has its input renames left unchecked, and one with a `compute_outputs` hook its output renames, since those fields aren't known until a graph is compiled.
- `registry.upgrade(record, node_id, *, to=None)` moves one node of a record to a version, and returns a `GraphRecord`. What it can't do raises `InvalidCallError`.
- Compiling never upgrades. A graph record that names an old version runs that version.
- `Deprecation(header=, description=, alternative=, migration=)`, given as `deprecation=` on its `@node`, marks a version that is going away. Its `alternative` is a node id, for a person to read.

**A graph as a node.** A graph record can be a node too, called a subgraph: `subgraph("enrich", title="Enrich", description="...")(record)`.

- It takes `replaces=` and `version=` like any node. It takes no `policy` and no hook, since its nodes run by their own.
- `registry.subgraph(...)` takes the same arguments, and adds the node to the registry.
- From outside, it is one node. Its inputs and outputs are the ones its graph declares, by their names there (`text`, `result`).
- Its inner nodes run inside every loop the subgraph node is inside. "The graph record" has the rest.

### Field Hooks

Some inputs and outputs depend on how a graph sets a node up. One node adds as many inputs as a constant says. Another has one output per name in a list. A hook works these out:

```python
def operand_inputs(count: int) -> dict:          # inputs to ADD; the function takes them as **values
    return {f"value_{i}": float for i in range(count)}


def branch_outputs(names: str, value: type) -> dict:   # all the outputs; value: the type arriving on "value"
    return {name: Annotated[value, Param(exclusive_group="branches")] for name in names.split(",")}
```

- A hook is a plain function, given per version as `compute_added_inputs=` or `compute_outputs=` on `@node`. It is called when a graph is compiled, never per call.
- `compute_added_inputs` returns the inputs to add, and the node's function takes them as `**values`. `compute_outputs` returns all the outputs.
- Each parameter of a hook names an input, and gets that input's constant, else its declared default.
- A parameter annotated `type` gets the type arriving on that input by its edge, and `Any` until an edge brings one. `**added: type` on `compute_outputs` gets the type arriving on each input that `compute_added_inputs` added.
- A table arriving is `Table[R]` or a bare `Table`. So `typing.get_args(table)` is its record type `R`, or empty.
- If an input the hook reads gets no value, the hook is not called, and the node's own problem says why.
- A hook returns `{name: type hint}`, read like a signature. For a field with a default it returns `{name: (type hint, default)}`, as pydantic's `create_model` takes one.
- Each field it returns is held to the same rules `@node` holds a parameter to (an input) or a returned field to (an output). So these are the hook's failure: an added input with an `exclusive_group` or the default `SKIPPED`, and an output of an `exclusive_group` with a default other than `SKIPPED`.
- A hook that raises is never an exception. It is the problem `compute_hook_failed` on the node: a `NodeError` keeps its code in `ctx.error` and its message, and any other exception is the variant `raised`, with its class name in `ctx.error` and its text in the `conductor` log. So is a field it gives a name a graph can't have: the problem is at that name, with `ctx.error` `not_a_name`.
- A hook that raises `NodeError` gives the problem its message, its `code` as `ctx.error`, and its own `ctx` whole as `ctx.error_ctx`.
- `graph.describe()` shows each node's fields as its hooks made them.

### A node for any type

A node can work for any type by using type variables: `def keep[T](value: T) -> T`, or `def split[T](value: Table[T] | list[T]) -> Series[T]`. A frozen dataclass of outputs may be generic too, with one output per field.

- A variable is the type that arrives on the edge. It is the same in every input and in the return, and it is decided when the graph is compiled. After that the node has ordinary inputs and outputs, and its output is checked against the bound type.
- Only an edge binds a variable. A constant, a default and a graph input bind nothing. A variable that nothing binds reads as its bound (`T: int | float`), else as `Any`.
- One or many is decided first. So a `Series[X]` wired to `value: T` runs per item, with `T` as `X`.
- In a union, the member shaped like the arriving type binds.
- At `T | None`, `T` is what arrives, without its `None`. The same goes for a bare `T`: `value: T` gets no `None`, since the node isn't called for one. A node that passes `None` on writes `T | None`.
- Two places for one variable join: `int` at one and `str` at the other make it `int | str`.
- What arrives outside a bound is `type_mismatch`.
- At `@node`, a variable on no input is `type_variable_only_in_return`, and a constrained one (`T: (int, str)`) is `type_variable_constrained`.
- A hook stays the way to say what a type can't: outputs named by a constant, or a record computed from other records.

### Types

Any type pydantic can check and write as JSON travels on edges: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `date`, `datetime`, a pydantic model or a dataclass of your own, or a `TypedDict`. A `TypedDict` is a record. It names a table's columns, and on its own it travels as one row of a table. A class of your own is declared first (see "How a type is named"): a plain class on a field, with no declaration, is `type_not_named`.

**Annotated metadata.** `Annotated` metadata that is not a `Param` is pydantic's. So `Annotated[int, annotated_types.Gt(0)]`, pydantic's own `pydantic.PositiveInt` and `constr(min_length=1)` are read as pydantic reads them. Two things there are refused:

- A widget (`widget_outside_param`). It goes on `Param(widget=...)`.
- Pydantic's `pydantic.Field(...)` (`pydantic_field_in_hint`). `Param` is the one way to give an input or an output its title, description and limits: write `Annotated[int, Param(ge=0)]`, never `Annotated[int, pydantic.Field(ge=0)]`. That holds on a parameter, on the return type, on an item of a `Series`, list or dict, and on a column of a table's row type.
- `pydantic.Field(...)` on the fields of a model or dataclass of your own is that class's business, and is fine. A union is told apart with `pydantic.Discriminator("kind")`.

**What lands where.** An edge joins an output to an input when the output's type lands on the input's.

- A subtype lands where its parent is asked for, and an `int` lands on a `float`.
- A `Literal` lands on a `Literal` that has all its values.
- A generic is compared by its arguments too: `list[int]` lands on `list[float]`, and never on `list[str]`.
- A type alias (`type X = ...`, or pydantic's JsonValue) is read as what it stands for. Text, a number, a yes or no, or a list or dict of them lands on a JsonValue; a model or a date does not. An alias takes `None` when what it stands for does.

**A yes or no is not a number.** A `bool` never lands on an `int` or `float` input. It doesn't land on a union that has a number and no `bool` (`int | float`, `int | str`) either, or on a host's subclass of a number, whatever its `accepts` says. Nor does it land as an item of a list, dict or `Series` of numbers.

- It is refused by an edge (`type_mismatch`), as a constant (`invalid_value`), and from a caller (`invalid_input`).
- It is refused in a table's `int` or `float` column: returned (`invalid_output`), brought by an edge (`invalid_edge_value`) or given (`invalid_input`).
- `true` read from JSON is refused for a number in the same way. That covers a person's answer (`invalid_answer`) and a saved run handed to `Run.from_json` (`saved_run_unreadable`). The reason is the same as for a caller's `True`: "a yes or no is not a number".

**How a type is named.** What a person sees for a type is declared, never guessed.

- Conductor's own types take their id and title from one fixed table. They are the builtins, decimals, dates, times, durations, UUIDs, dicts, lists, tuples, sets and `Any`. `str` is titled "Text", `int` "Whole number", `float` "Number" and `bool` "Yes or no".
- A type of your own, on a field or a table's column, is declared with `@host_type("money", title="Money", accepts=[...])` above the class. Put it above `@dataclass` when there is one. For a library's class, write `host_type("ip", title="IP address")(the_class)`.
- The id is the name an editor and a graph record know the type by. The title is what a person reads.
- The declaration is checked when the class statement ends. `type_declaration_invalid` is any of these: an id that isn't one word or is one of conductor's own; an empty title; `accepts` with something other than classes in it; `@host_type` on a function or a `TypedDict`; a class that can't take a new attribute. `type_not_supported` is a class pydantic can't validate, declared or inside a record.
- A class with no declaration fails where its node is declared (`type_not_named`). A subclass declares its own.
- `@host_type` is a decorator, not a base class, because a base class runs before the class is finished. That breaks a generic pydantic model, `@dataclass(slots=True)` and enums. And a library's class can't be given a base class.
- A class's own fields named `id` or `title` stay its own.
- A `TypedDict` declares nothing. Its id is `record`, and a table's id names its columns: `Table[name: str, email: str | None]`.
- A generic is known by its class and its arguments: `dict[str, int]`, or a bare `list` for `list[Any]`. So a class of your own inside one is declared too. A generic pydantic model declared as `box` is `box[int]` with an `int` inside.
- A `Literal` is known by its values' types, a union by its members, and a type alias by its name.
- `accepts=[...]` lists the other classes whose values may land on the type. The type reads such a value itself.
- A subclass of a builtin, such as `class Text(str)`, needs only its declaration. A value is validated as the builtin, then made the subclass. A class that needs another way gives its own `__get_pydantic_core_schema__`.

**The types of a registry.**

- `registry.types` is every class its nodes' field types name, by id, plus `NodeRegistry(types=[...])`. That is each member of a union, a `Literal`'s value types, and a generic's class and its arguments'; but not `Any`, `None`, a type alias or a table. One id claimed by two classes raises (`duplicate_type_id`).
- `registry.describe().types` is a list with an entry per type. Each entry's `accepted_as` is the ids a value of that type may land on.

**`Series[X]`** is many values of one type. To the node and to a type checker it is a plain list. A `polars.Series` returned for one is read as its values, though a type checker wants `series.to_list()`. A `list[X]` stays one value that is a list.

**`Table[R]`** is a whole table as one value, a `polars.DataFrame` at run time. A `TypedDict` `R` names its columns, and a column's `Param` limits are held. A bare `Table` has any columns.

- It is a type like any other. It can be a member of a union (`Table[R] | list[T]`), an item of a `Series` (`Series[Table[R]]`) and a field of a record.
- A table is read from a frame, or from a list of records with one object per row. That holds wherever it comes from: a caller, a person's answer, collected records, or a node's own return.
- Once read, a `Table[R]` has exactly `R`'s columns: each one is there, and others are cut. So a node that passes on columns it doesn't name returns a bare `Table`.
- A table with no rows has every declared column.
- As JSON a table is `{"columns": [{"name", "type", "values"}]}`, with its columns in order. `type` is the word for the cells: `bool`, `int`, `float`, `str`, `date`, `datetime`, `time`, `timedelta`, a decimal's class name, or else `json`. This is how a table is written in a default, in a waiting call's inputs and in a saved run.
- Every cell of a table a run keeps reads back from `Run.from_json` as it was. A column with no value at all (empty, or every cell null) may read back with another type, since no cell says which.

Wherever a table arrives (a node's return, a caller, a person's answer, an edge), each column is converted to the type a saved run reads it back as, when no cell changes. The run keeps the converted table.

- Every whole-number type becomes Int64. A UInt64 does too when every cell fits, and is refused otherwise.
- Float32 becomes Float64, and a Categorical or Enum becomes String.
- A Datetime or Duration becomes microseconds. That holds for one in milliseconds, and for one in nanoseconds when every cell is a whole microsecond.
- A Decimal becomes precision 38, and a fixed-size Array becomes a List.
- A list or struct of these is converted the same way inside.

A column that would read back changed is refused, naming the column and the type to cast it to. That is `invalid_output`, `invalid_input`, `invalid_answer` or `invalid_edge_value`, by where the table arrived. Such columns are:

- a Datetime in a time zone other than UTC;
- bytes;
- a list or struct holding a date, a time, a decimal (written as text) or a float that isn't finite;
- a UInt64 past the largest Int64;
- a time finer than a microsecond, and a millisecond time too far out for microseconds.

Records given for a table, and a column whose JSON form is `json`, are read the way polars reads rows. It finds one type for each column and converts every cell to it. So `1` and `2.5` become floats, `True` and `2` become `1` and `2`, and `"x"` and `2` become text.

A column may have a `None` only where its type says `| None`. A table with a `None` in any other column is refused where it arrives, naming the column (`invalid_output`, `invalid_input`, `invalid_edge_value`).

To a type checker, a `Table[R]` is a frame that names `R`. Frame methods need no narrowing, and a node may return a plain `polars.DataFrame`. A checker shows `R` (`reveal_type`, `assert_type`). But it accepts a table of one record type where another is expected, because the type includes a plain `polars.DataFrame`.

### The graph record

A graph record is a graph as data. A graph declares what it takes and what it returns, the way a function declares its parameters and its return value.

`GraphRecord(nodes={id: NodeRecord, ...}, outputs={name: Source, ...})` is stored like this:

```json
{"nodes": {"b": {"node": "b", "inputs": {"text": {"sources": [{"node": "a", "output": "result"}]}}}},
 "outputs": {"result": {"node": "b", "output": "result"}}}
```

- `NodeRecord(node=, version=1, inputs=, display=)` is one node of the graph. `node` is the id of the node it uses. Empty fields, and a `version` of 1, are left out when it is saved.
- Each input's entry is one of three kinds: `InputEntry(constant=)`, `InputEntry(graph_input=, default=)` or `InputEntry(sources=(Source(node, output, field=None), ...))`.
- A dict of the same shape is read too: `GraphRecord.model_validate(data)`.
- A graph input exists only where an entry names it, and a graph output only in `outputs`. Used as a subgraph, these are the node's inputs and outputs.
- Constants, defaults and a node's `display` are JSON values. `make_graph` writes a Python value as its JSON: a date as its ISO text, an enum as its value, and a float that isn't finite as its text, `"NaN"` or `"Infinity"`. So a record equals what its JSON reads back as. A record built with a float that isn't finite in it is refused.
- A value with no JSON form, such as a `polars.DataFrame`, is `invalid_value` at the call. Give a table as a list of records instead.
- A node id, an input, an output and a graph port are names. A name is not empty, and has no `.`, `/`, `@` or `~`.
- The record keeps no order of its nodes. Where order matters, nodes are taken by id.

**What an input's entry says.**

- An edge is a source on the input it leads into: `{"node": "a", "output": "result"}`. Add `"field": "email"` to read one field of the record that output gives.
  - Several sources of one input are alternatives (see "One or many"). A source listed twice is refused (`invalid_record`).
  - A source naming a node the graph doesn't have is `edge_names_missing_node`.
  - A graph output naming a node the graph doesn't have, or an output its node doesn't have, is `graph_output_not_found`, with `loc` `()` and `ctx` `output`, `source` and `outputs`.
- `{"constant": v}` is the input's value on every call of every run. The graph doesn't offer that input to a caller.
- `{"graph_input": name}` is the caller's value, under that name. `{"graph_input": name, "default": v}` adds a value for when the caller gives none.
  - The default is the record's. `{"graph_input": name}` with no `default` is required, whatever the input's own default.
  - Several inputs may name one graph input, and the caller's one value feeds them all.
  - Two of them must agree, else they are `graph_input_used_two_ways`. They clash when they read different types from their hints (a different type, limits, choices or validators), are shown differently (a different title, description or widget), or have different record defaults.
  - `int` and `Annotated[int, Param()]` agree. But `Annotated[int, annotated_types.Ge(0)]` and `Annotated[int, Param(ge=0)]`, one rule written two ways, are read as two types and clash, though both take the same values.
- An entry has exactly one of `constant`, `graph_input` and `sources` (`invalid_record`, `ctx.error` `one_of_constant_graph_input_sources`). It has `default` only beside `graph_input` (`default_without_graph_input`).
- With nothing set, the input takes its declared default. A required input with nothing set, on any node, is `input_has_no_value`.
- `display` is the host's own. It is stored, and never read. What a host keeps about the whole graph, such as a name or a viewport, it stores beside the record.

**One value or many.** The type decides, never the value.

- A list (a JSON array, a Python list or tuple) is refused for an input that takes one value of a type that takes no list. It is `invalid_input` when given, and `invalid_value` as a constant.
- An input whose own type takes a list (`list[str]`, `Series[...]`, `Table[...]`, `Any`) takes the list as one value.
- An open `Series` input takes only a list. One value given there is `invalid_input`.
- A set has no order, so it is never a list. A set given for a `Series` input is refused with `set_has_no_order` in the problem's `errors`. A `list[...]` or `Any` input takes a set as the value it is.
- `make_graph` and an upgrade's rewrite refuse a constant with a set anywhere in it, with `set_has_no_order` too. A set has no JSON form, so a record with a set in it, handed to `Graph.compile`, is `invalid_record`.

**A subgraph is one node.** Its inputs and outputs are the ones its graph declares, by their names there. So an author wires `emb.text`, and an edge from `emb.result`. No name has a dot.

- A subgraph node's inputs get their values from outside, as any node's do. A constant, a graph input or an edge in the outer graph takes the place of a default in the subgraph's own record.
- An inner input that takes only a constant (`constant_only`) is set inside the subgraph, and is not offered outside.
- A node outside reads a subgraph's output as it would read the same node drawn in its own graph.

For example, take the subgraph `documents -> lines -> shout`. `shout` is called once per line of each document, and its output is the subgraph's `result`.

- An input of one `str` wired to `emb.result` is called once per line.
- A `Series[str]` input wired to it is called once per document, with that document's lines. That is the list per document that `run.results` shows.

Loops inside a subgraph are named by the list inside that is looped over.

- `describe()` gives a node there the `per_item_of` `emb/documents.result`: the path of the node inside, then the output.
- Two outputs returned in the same loop inside line up. A node that takes one item of each is called once per item, with both values. A node that takes one value per document, beside a `Series` of that document's lines, is called once per document.
- Outputs returned in different loops inside don't line up: `series_not_nested`, with `ctx.variant` `inside_subgraph`. Its message says to give one whole to a `Series` input, or to return both from the same loop inside.

The description of such an output says `is_series`. Its `type`, `schema` and `choices` are those of the value the node inside returns (`str`). It lists its `loops` as their sources inside are written, outermost first: `["documents.result", "lines.result"]`. So this one is a list per document of a list per line.

- A field's value has one level of list per entry of `loops`, when it has any. Otherwise it has one level when it `is_series`, and none when it isn't. A `Series` the subgraph returns outside every loop has `loops` `[]`, and is one list.
- `loops` is empty for every field but a subgraph's output that is returned inside loops.
- A `Series` returned once per document is a `Series[Series[T]]` the same way, and a table returned once per document is a `Series` of tables.

Branches inside a subgraph work as they would drawn in the outer graph.

- An exclusive group inside is named by the path of its deciding node: `d.answer`, or `g/d.answer` for a node `d` inside a subgraph node `g`.
- Two outputs that depend on opposite branches of one decision inside are alternatives outside. Both may be wired into one input, and each call gets the value from the branch that was chosen. Collected into two `Series` inputs of one node, they are `lists_from_different_loops`.
- A `None`, or a branch not chosen, arriving at one of its inputs makes the inner nodes wired to it not called, or skipped. `run.not_called` lists those nodes.

A subgraph is compiled on its own, apart from the graph it is used in. So a type variable at one of its graph inputs has no edge to bind it, and reads as its bound, else `Any`.

- A subgraph whose first node is `series-split` offers `Table | list`, and gives records of unknown fields. The same nodes drawn in the outer graph would have the arriving table's fields.
- A first node whose input has a precise type (`Table[R]`, `R` a `TypedDict`) gives the subgraph that type.
- A `Series` input inside a subgraph collects only the loops inside that graph. Wired to a value returned once inside, it is a list of one, whatever loop the subgraph node is inside outside.

Using a graph as a subgraph changes nothing about how its nodes behave.

- Each inner node is called by its own `Policy`. Its `concurrency`, when set, counts its calls in the whole process, across every item the subgraph node runs for. Its retries and `attempt_timeout` are its own. The subgraph takes no `Policy`.
- A cancel and the `timeout` of `resume()` stop the inner nodes as they stop any node.
- `run.again` reuses the previous run's outcomes node by node.
- `results` and `describe()` show the subgraph as one node. Its outputs are its graph's outputs, by name, each what the inner node behind it returned. It is never called itself, so a subgraph costs what its nodes cost.
- It says `node_start` when the first node inside starts, and `node_complete` once every node inside has completed. Its `outcomes` is the number of items it runs for, and `skipped` the number of those whose every call inside was skipped. It has no `node_progress`.

What is inside a subgraph is told with where it is.

- A problem's `loc` starts with the node and item of each subgraph around it: `("emb", 1, "upper")`.
- A compile problem of the subgraph is its own problem, behind the subgraph node's id: `("emb", "upper", "text")`.
- A `Waiting` and a `NotCalled` have the same `loc`, and a waiting id spells it `emb@1/ask~3fa2c0d1`.
- An inner node says its events once, as any node that runs per item does. Their `loc` has the ids of the subgraph nodes around it in front: `("emb", "upper")`.

### Writing a graph in Python

`make_graph(*nodes, edges=None, constants={}, defaults={}, inputs={}, outputs={})` writes a `GraphRecord` from Python. It writes the record and compiles nothing.

```python
chained = Graph.compile(make_graph(lines, upper, join), registry)    # the quick start's graph, as a chain
print(chained.run(text="a\nb").outputs)  # {'result': 'A+B'}

record = make_graph(upper, join, constants={"upper.text": "x"})
print(record.nodes["upper"].inputs["text"].constant)  # x
```

**Node ids.** Each node is written at its version, under its own id. That is the id given with it, as in `make_graph(("a", upper), ("b", upper))`, or else its definition's. A definition used twice gets `upper-1` and `upper-2`.

**A chain.** With no `edges`, the nodes form a chain. Each node gets an edge from the one output of the node before it, into its one required input that has no constant or default and that the edge can feed.

- When that can't be drawn, it is `not_a_chain`. When the only required inputs left take only a constant, it is `not_a_chain` with the variant `constant_only` and `ctx.inputs`.
- By itself, `make_graph` never wires an input that takes only a constant, or makes it a graph input. Compiled without a constant, such an input is `input_has_no_value`, variant `constant_only`.
- `edges=`, `defaults=` or `inputs=` that do wire one are written as given, for compiling to refuse (`input_takes_only_a_constant`).
- A chain reads the fields each node declares. A subgraph, or a node whose fields a hook works out, takes `edges=`.

**Edges.** `edges=[("upper.result", "join.texts")]` lists every edge, and nothing is matched by name. `"read.result.email"` is the field `email` of the record `read` returns.

**Constants and defaults.** `constants={"upper.text": "x"}` gives inputs constants, the same on every call of every run. `defaults=` makes inputs graph inputs, with values the caller may change.

**The graph's inputs and outputs.** `make_graph` declares them.

- The graph inputs are every required input that gets nothing (no edge, no constant), on any node, named by the input. Every key of `defaults` is one too.
- An optional input that gets nothing takes its own default, and is no graph input.
- The graph outputs are every output of the nodes no edge leaves, named by the output.
- `inputs=` and `outputs=` give some of them other names: `inputs={"who": "greet.name"}`, `inputs={"text": ["a.text", "b.text"]}` (one graph input feeding both), `outputs={"long": "join.result"}`. A field named there is declared under that name, and the other automatic ones stay. So `outputs={}` still declares every automatic output.
- Two graph inputs that would share a name, automatic or named in `inputs=`, raise `graph_inputs_share_a_name` (`ctx.inputs`). Two graph outputs raise `graph_outputs_share_a_name` (`ctx.outputs`).
- A field a hook adds or returns is known only when the graph is compiled. So a graph input or output on one is named in `inputs=` or `outputs=`.

**What it raises.** `make_graph` raises one `InvalidCallError` that lists everything it can't write:

- a place that names a node it wasn't given, in any argument: an edge, a constant, a default, `inputs=` or `outputs=` (`node_not_in_graph`);
- a value with no JSON form, or with a set in it (`invalid_value`);
- a place that isn't `"node.name"` (`invalid_place`). Its `loc` is the argument and where in it: `("edges", 1, 0)` or `("constants", key)`;
- two graph inputs or two graph outputs of one name;
- what the record refuses (`invalid_record`, with `ctx.written_by` `make_graph's arguments`): an input given a constant and an edge, an edge written twice, one id given to two nodes, a field on a graph output;
- a chain it can't draw (`not_a_chain`).

An argument of the wrong type, such as `outputs=None` or an edge that isn't a pair of texts, is a mistake in the calling code, not in the graph. It raises a `TypeError` that names the argument, before anything else is checked.

Everything else is in `Graph.compile(record, registry).problems`: an input or output a node doesn't have, a value its field refuses, an input that gets nothing, an edge between types that don't meet, a graph half drawn.

### Compiling

`Graph.compile(record, registry)` checks a graph record against the nodes it uses, and makes a `Graph`. It takes a `GraphRecord`, its JSON text, or that JSON as plain data (a dict).

It never raises for a fault in the graph. Each fault is a `Problem` (`type`, `loc`, `msg`, `ctx`) in `graph.problems`, and `graph.is_runnable` says whether there are none.

**Faults in the shape raise.** The rule: the shape is the call's, and what the shape says is the graph's. What doesn't have a record's shape raises `InvalidCallError`, with one `invalid_record` problem per fault. Its `loc` is `("record", *where)`, and pydantic's code is in `ctx.error`. That covers:

- text that isn't JSON (`json_invalid`);
- a key a record doesn't have, such as `vaules`, or `type` for `node`;
- a field of the wrong type;
- a key written twice in one JSON object, such as two nodes with one id (`repeated_key`);
- a node id, input or port that is not a name (`not_a_name`), and a field that is empty or starts with `.` (`not_a_field`);
- a source listed twice (`repeated_source`), and an empty list of sources (`no_sources`);
- an entry of no kind or of two (`one_of_constant_graph_input_sources`), and a `default` without `graph_input` (`default_without_graph_input`);
- a field on a graph output (`output_has_field`).

The `loc` goes down to the fault. An entry of no kind or of two ends at its input, `("record", "nodes", "b", "inputs", "text")`. A fault inside an entry goes on, as `("record", "nodes", "b", "inputs", "text", "sources")` for a source listed twice. A node id or input that is not a name ends in `"[key]"`. A record that `make_graph` or an `Upgrade` wrote says so in `ctx.written_by`. Its message ends "Fix make_graph's arguments." or "Fix the Upgrade of 'split' to version 2.".

`read_json(text)` reads JSON text as data, with every object's keys seen. For a key written twice, or text that is not JSON, it raises `InvalidCallError` of `invalid_record`, with `ctx.error` `repeated_key` or `json_invalid`.

**The graph.**

- The graph keeps its own copy of the definitions it resolved, so a later change to the registry doesn't reach it.
- A graph that uses subgraphs made for one request is compiled with a registry of its own: a new `NodeRegistry`, then `add_subregistry(shared)`, then `add(*definitions)`. `docs/subgraphs.md` teaches it.
- `graph.inputs` is the graph inputs the record declares, by name. Each is the `FieldDescription` a caller gives a value for. Its `default` is the record's default as JSON, and is absent when it is `required`.
- A graph input with no value yet is not a problem. A required input that gets nothing is `input_has_no_value`.
- `graph.outputs` is the names of the graph outputs the record declares.

**`graph.describe()`** is the graph as an editor draws it, a `GraphDescription`. It has each node's fields as its hooks made them (an output's `exclusive_group` among them), how often each node runs, the inputs, the outputs and the problems.

- How often a node runs is its `per_item_of`: the list of the innermost loop it is inside, or `None` for a node called once.
- It is written as the list's node path and output: `lines.result`, or `per-word/split.result` for the list `split.result` returned inside the subgraph node `per-word`. That is a place inside the subgraph that no edge of this graph names, and that is not a key of `nodes`.
- A graph is compiled once. How often each node runs is the same for every run of it, whatever a run is given.
- Each input of a node says where it gets its value on each call, as its `source`, an `InputSource` with a `mode` and a `series`. The modes are:
  - `constant`: written in the record, or the default;
  - `graph_input`: the caller's value;
  - `one_value`: the output of a node called once;
  - `item`: one item of a Series;
  - `outer_value`: returned outside the loop the node is inside;
  - `collected`: every item of a Series.
- A node with a problem is drawn with its fields all the same, and so is a node that reads it. An input whose edge is refused has the mode `missing`.
- A `type_mismatch` names its input in its `loc`. A `cycle` and `series_not_nested` name the node.
- Only a node whose fields aren't known has `found` false, no fields and no `per_item_of`. That is an `unknown_node`, an `unknown_version`, `subgraph_contains_itself`, a hook that failed, a hook that wasn't called for a value it reads (`input_has_no_value` or `input_takes_only_a_constant` on that input), and a subgraph with problems of its own.
- The inner nodes of such a subgraph are not compiled into the graph. Its problems are the graph's, each `loc` the subgraph node's id and then the place inside it: `("e", "x")`.

**Other codes.**

- `unknown_node` and `unknown_version`.
- `unknown_input`: an entry names an input the node lacks.
- `unknown_output`: an edge or a graph output names an output, or a field of a record output, that the node doesn't give.
- `type_mismatch`: an edge between types that don't meet.
- `invalid_value`: a constant or default its type refuses. Its variant `bound_default` is a declared default that doesn't fit the type an edge gives a type variable.
- `compute_hook_failed`: see "Field Hooks". `context_does_not_fit`: see "Context".
- `input_has_no_value` and `graph_input_used_two_ways`.
- `cycle`.
- `subgraph_contains_itself`, on the node that closes the circle.
- `input_takes_only_a_constant`: an edge or a graph input into an input that takes only a constant.

### What a node returns

What a node returns is read strictly, by its declared type.

- A value of exactly that class is taken as it is. A model may come back as a dict.
- But `"no"` is never a `bool`, `"12"` never an `int`, a date's text never a `date`, and `12.0` never an `int` column.
- `True` is never a number, wherever a value is read: an `int` or `float` input, an item of a list or a `Series`, a field of a `TypedDict`, or a cell of a table (`bool_is_not_a_number`).
- The fields of your own pydantic model or dataclass are read strictly too, whatever the model's own config says. So `{"a": "1"}` for a model with `a: int` is refused, and `True` there is pydantic's `int_type`.
- A fault fails that call of the node as `invalid_output`, with `ctx` `name`, `reason`, `errors` and, for a table, `column`. It quotes nothing of the value.

**What an edge carries.** Sometimes an input asks for more than its source's type promises: a limit on the input, an `int` into a `float`, or a host type's own check. Then the value the edge carries is read by the input, as a constant is. A value it refuses is `invalid_edge_value` on the node it reached, with `ctx` `name`, `reason`, `errors` and, for a table, `column`.

A table wired to a table input is checked when compiling, by each column the input declares whose type the source knows (`type_mismatch`, see "One or many"). A table of unknown columns is checked when it arrives.

### One or many

A node's types say how many values it deals with.

- `text: str` is one value.
- `Series[str]` is many values of one type, called a series. Each value in it is an item.
- A `list[str]` is one value, and so is a table.

In the quick start, `lines` returns a `Series[str]`, `upper` takes one text, and `join` takes a `Series[str]`. Each time conductor runs a node's function is one call. A call's result, its outcome, is what the run keeps.

**A loop.** A `Series[T]` output wired to an input that takes one `T` starts a loop. That node is called once per item, each call with its own item, and so is every node downstream of it.

- Only a `Series` or `Table` input takes a series whole. Every other input takes it one item at a time, an `Any` input included.
- The `per_item_of` of a node in `graph.describe()` says which series it runs per item of.

**A field of a record.** An edge may name one field of a record that an output returns (a `TypedDict`, a pydantic model or a dataclass), one level down: `{"node": "series-split", "output": "result", "field": "email"}`, written `series-split.result.email` in `make_graph`.

- It works on one record, or on each item of a series of them.
- A field of a record of unknown fields is `Any`, and is read when it arrives.
- A name the record lacks is `unknown_output`, which lists its fields.

**An outer value.** A node upstream of the series may return a value outside the loop. That value is the same on every call inside the loop: the document's name, say, on each call for one of its lines. Nothing is copied.

**Collecting.** A `Series[T]` input wired to a node inside a loop collects the loop. It gets every `T` that node returned, in item order, and its own node is called once for all of them.

- Wired to a node that is called once, it gets that one value as a list of one.
- Another input may put the collecting node inside a loop itself. Say it also collects what was returned per line, and so runs per document. Then each call gets only what was returned for its own document, never every document's.
- A `Series` output wired to a `Series` input is passed whole.

A `Table` input collects records the same way.

- A `Table[R]` input wired to records collects them into a table.
- Wired to a table, it takes that table.
- Wired to a `Series` of tables (a `Series[Table[R]]` output, or a table returned per item inside a subgraph), it takes one table per item, so its node runs once per item. A `Series[Table[R]]` input collects the tables.
- A bare `Table` input collects records of any columns: items that are a `dict`, a `TypedDict` or `Any`.
- A value declared `Any` is read as a table only where it is returned once in the graph, with no loop to collect. Returned per item, it is a record, so declare a table as one.
- A text, a number or any other value that is no record is `type_mismatch`, as it is into `Table[R]`.

**Loops inside loops.** A node inside a loop may itself return a `Series`. Each document has lines of its own, so the loop over the lines is inside the loop over the documents.

- A call's item indexes are one index per loop, outermost first. `(0, 3)` is the fourth line of the first document.
- Collecting ends the innermost loop only. A node that collects the lines runs once per document, and a node that collects that runs once.

**Nested, or refused.** A node runs per item of the innermost series its inputs come from. Every other input must come from that series, from a series it is inside, or from outside them all.

- Items of two series that are not one inside the other never pair up: `series_not_nested`.
- To fix it, make one inside the other. Take ten documents and three questions written in the graph: wire the document into the node that returns the questions, so each document has its three questions.
- Or give one of them whole to a `Series` input. There it is an outer value beside the other's items.

**A table is one value.** It never starts a loop, and a column of it is no source.

- A node that returns `Series[R]` returns its records one item each. `series-split` in `syv-conductor-nodes` does that for any table or list.
- Such a node may return the records as a list, or as the table itself. A table returned for `Series[R]`, `R` a `TypedDict`, is read as a `Table[R]` is: its columns, each by its type, with a `None` only where the type takes one. It is kept by column. An edge that names a field (`series-split.result.email`) reads the column, and a node still receives plain `dict` records.
- A table returned for `Series[Any]` gives every column.
- Every field of a row type is required. A `NotRequired` field, or a `TypedDict` declared `total=False`, is refused when the node is declared (`row_field_optional`). Declare the field `X | None`. A table with a column some rows leave out is not supported.
- A whole table or list wired to an input of one value is `type_mismatch`, with `ctx.variant` `make_a_series` (`kind`, `fields`). A field named on one is `unknown_output`, with the same hint.

**Which tables fit.**

- A table fits a `Table[R]` input when it has every column `R` names, each of a type that fits. One it lacks is `type_mismatch` with `ctx.variant` `add_column` (`column`, `column_type`, `has`).
- A `Table[R]` input receives exactly the columns `R` names, whether the table was wired, given or collected.
- A `Table[R]` output is cut to `R`'s columns too. A bare `Table` output keeps every column it returns.
- A table written as the constant of a `Table` input, or given for one by a caller, is a frame or a list of records, and `[]` is a table of no rows. Each column `R` names is read by its own type (a date from its ISO text, a host type from its own text), and other columns are left out. A missing column, or a cell its type refuses, is `invalid_value` as a constant and `invalid_input` when given, with `ctx.column` naming it.

**Several edges into one input are alternatives,** for a `Series` input as for any other.

- Each must be on its own branch of one node: outputs that share an `exclusive_group`, or nodes downstream of them. So a call gets at most one. Otherwise it is `several_edges_into_one_input`.
- They must be inside the same loops, or they are `alternatives_from_different_loops`.
- Opposite branches into one `Series` input are collected as one list, in item order.
- Whole tables on opposite branches into one `Table` input give the one whose branch was chosen.

**What collecting leaves out.** Three rules.

1. A `Series` input gets the items that have a value, in order.
   - An item with none (`None`, or its branch not chosen) is left out of every `Series` input of the node together. So two `Series` inputs wired to one loop stay paired. `Series[T | None]` keeps the item's place as `None`.
   - A `Series` output passed whole lines up with them the same way.
   - A `Table` input keeps no place, since a record is never `None`.
   - No items is an empty list, and the node is called with it.
   - Two `Series[X]` inputs wired to opposite branches of one node would lose every item: `lists_from_different_loops`.
2. Only what was decided per item is left out. Before looking at any item, the collecting node asks one question of what is decided outside the loop: could any item have a value here?
   - The answers are ordered: skipped, then `None`, then "could have a value".
   - An outer value is read as it is.
   - A node inside the loop is the worst of its inputs, where an input that takes `None` receives it. An input is the best of its alternative edges. An output in an `exclusive_group` of a node that isn't called is skipped.
   - When no item could have a value, the collecting node is treated like any node wired there, with two items as with none. It is skipped when the cause is a branch not chosen, and not called when the cause is a `None`. `Series[T] | None` then receives `None`. `Series[T | None]`, which takes `None` per item, is called with a `None` in each item's place.
   - A series that was never returned has no items, so it is the input's own `None`. A node that chooses a branch from an item of it chooses none, which skips what collects that branch. But downstream of a node that takes `None`, the choosing node could be called, so what collects its branch isn't called, as for any `None`.
   - A list of one is read the same way: its one value, `None` or not, is its one item.
   - When an item could have a value, each item answers for itself by rule 1. A branch chosen per item, or a `None` item, leaves only that item out.
3. A collecting node waits until every item has an outcome.

**Skipping one item.** `SKIPPED` for one item leaves a gap there (`None` in `run.results`), and the nodes wired to it are skipped for that item. Outside a loop, it skips the nodes wired to it.

**The item limit.** `graph.run(max_items=1000)` limits how many items any one series a loop runs over may have.

- It is checked when the series is returned, before any call for its items.
- A series that is only collected or passed whole is not counted.
- Over the limit, the run stops (`status` `stopped`) with the problem `item_limit` (`series`, `items`, `max_items`). Its `loc` is the call that returned the series, the loc a failure of that call has: `("lines", 1)` for the second call of `lines`.
- `run.with_max_items(...).resume()` goes on under a higher limit, calling nothing again.

**Subgraphs.** A subgraph's inner nodes are inside every loop its node is inside. A `Series` input inside it collects only loops inside the subgraph.

### Asking a person

A node can stop and ask a person for a value, such as an approval or a reason.

`run.resume()` calls every node that is ready until the run is complete, waits for a person, or ends early: failed, stopped, cancelled or timed out. Then it returns the `Run`. `graph.run` does the same from the start. `status` says how it stopped: `complete`, `waiting`, `failed`, `stopped`, `cancelled` or `timed_out`. For the last four, `cause` is the `Problem` that ended it. The other two statuses, `ready` and `running`, are under "Running".

A node asks by raising `Ask(prompt, choices=, default=)`, and says it may with `asks=True` on its `@node`. What is asked is what the node returns. So its return type says the answer's shape and how to ask. How a question looks (title, description, widget) is its `Param`, as for an input. `-> str` with a bare `raise Ask(prompt)` is a free-text question.

The call that asked, and every call downstream of it, wait. The rest of the graph runs on, and the run ends `waiting`:

```python
@registry.node("approve", title="Approve", description="Asks a person whether to approve an invoice.", asks=True)
def approve(invoice: str) -> bool:
    raise Ask(f"Approve {invoice}?")


approving = Graph.compile(make_graph(approve, constants={"approve.invoice": "INV-1"}), registry)
paused = approving.run()                                 # paused.status == "waiting"
answered = paused.answer(paused.waiting[0], True)        # raises here if wrong; no node runs
finished = answered.resume()
again = Run.from_json(finished.to_json(), approving)           # a run is JSON
```

**Declaring it.**

- A node that raises `Ask` says `asks=True`. It is answered with a value of its return type. The answer is its outputs, and the node is not called again for that call.
- A node that raises `Ask` without `asks=True` fails the call as `ask_not_declared`. So `describe().asks` is certain for every node. A host needs to know before it runs a graph unattended whether a call may wait for a person.
- A node that needs a person's answer reads it from an edge, as it reads any value. "Approve, then pay" is two nodes. `approval(invoice: str) -> bool`, declared `asks=True`, returns `True` for a small invoice and raises `Ask` for a large one. `pay(invoice: str, ok: bool) -> str` reads `approval.result`. `pay` is called once, with a real `bool`.
- A host that offers the two as one palette entry makes them a `subgraph`. Its waiting call is then `approve_and_pay/approval~...`.

**What the return type asks.**

- `bool` asks for a yes or no.
- `Literal["low", "high"]` asks for one of its values.
- `str`, `int`, `float` and `date` ask for a value.
- A frozen dataclass is a form of one question per field. A field's default is proposed. A field whose default is `SKIPPED` proposes nothing, and left out of the answer it is a branch not chosen.
- `Table[R]` is a table answered as records. It is read as a caller's table is, but each cell strictly from its JSON form: other columns are dropped, and a missing column is refused.
- `Series[X]` asks for several values. So `Series[Literal[...]]`, or `Series[str]` with `choices`, is a pick of several.
- A hook's output types ask the same way.

**What `Ask` adds.** `Ask` adds what only the run knows.

- On a node of one output, `choices=[...]` gives the question choices, each a value or a `Choice(id, title)`. `default=` proposes an answer.
- Each has the answer's shape. So on a node of several outputs, each goes by output name: `choices={output: [...]}`, `default={output: value}`.
- An `Ask` that doesn't fit the outputs fails the node as `invalid_ask`, with `ctx.reason`. That is:
  - a default or choice its type refuses, or a default an answer couldn't be;
  - a default for an output of an `exclusive_group`, which, left out, is a branch not chosen;
  - no choices, or one choice given twice;
  - a name that isn't an output;
  - the one-output form on several outputs, or a `choices` mapping on one output.
- On one output, a `default` that is a mapping is read as the default value itself, so `default={"result": 1}` on `-> dict` proposes `{"result": 1}`.
- Choices on a `Table` output are whole tables.

**A waiting call.** Each entry of `run.waiting` is a `Waiting`:

- `id`, such as `approve@1~3fa2c0d1`: the node's id, then `@` and a number for each item it was called for, from the outside in, then `~` and a fingerprint of the call. A node that runs once is `approve` alone before the `~`. Inside a subgraph, the nodes are joined by `/`, each with the item index of its own loop: `review@0/approve@1~...`. The fingerprint is made from the node's id, its code and the call's inputs; the `Ask`'s prompt, choices and default are not in it.
- `loc`: the node, then its item, as a problem's `loc`.
- `prompt`.
- `inputs`: what the call received, as JSON.
- `questions`, one per output. Each is the field record `describe()` writes for the output (`name`, `title`, `is_series`, `type`, `schema`, `required`, ...). A question is titled as `describe()` titles its output: `Param(title=)` on the return type, else `None`.
- A question's `choices` are `Choice`s, written `[{"id", "title"}]`. They come from the `Ask`, else from the output's `Param(choices=)` or `Literal`.
- A question's `default` comes from the `Ask`, else from the output's own.
- `required` and `default` say what an answer that leaves the question out gives, as for any field. A `default` gives that value, with `null` meaning `None`. No `default` with `required` true is a fault. No `default` with `required` false is a branch not chosen.
- A node of one output is answered with its value, so its one question is always `required`. A `default` there, from the `Ask` or the output's type, is the value a host fills the answer in with: `run.answer(id, {})` is refused as `invalid_answer`.

**Answering.** `run.answer(waiting, value)` answers one waiting call, and `run.answer({waiting_id: value, ...})` answers several in one call. It returns a new run, and nothing runs until `resume()`.

- One question is answered with its value. Several (a node of several outputs) are answered with a mapping by output name.
- In the mapping, a question left out gives what it says: its `default`, else a branch not chosen when it is not `required`, else it is refused. So a question with a default may be left out, and so may one whose type takes `None` and that has no choices (its `default` is `null`).
- Of an `exclusive_group`, exactly one is answered. The others are branches not chosen.
- Each answer is read strictly from its JSON form: `true`, not `"yes"` or `1`; `3`, not `"3"`; a date as its ISO text. It is checked against its question before anything runs.
- Every fault is refused at once, and nothing is answered.
  - `invalid_answer` has `ctx.waiting_id`, `ctx.reason`, and `ctx.question` when it is about one question. It also covers one call answered twice in one `answer`.
  - `not_waiting` is for a call that is not waiting, with `ctx.waiting_id`, `ctx.status`, and `ctx.moved_to` when its question now waits on another call.
  - `answer_stale` is for an id whose place waits with another fingerprint: the call there got other inputs, as when `run.again` moved another item there, or the node's code changed. `ctx.current` is the id waiting there now, and `ctx.moved_to` is there when the old question now waits on another call. An id whose place waits on nothing is `not_waiting`.
- An id without its `~` part names the call alone, and answers whatever question waits there.
- A node that asked is not called again for that item.

**Declining.** `run.decline(waiting, reason=None)` declines to answer one waiting call. It takes the call as `run.answer` does, an entry of `run.waiting` or its id, and returns a new run.

- The call fails as a call whose node raised does: it has no outcome, and the run is `failed` with `answer_declined` as its `cause`. Nothing that reads its outputs is called. The other questions still wait, and an answer to one of them leaves the run `failed`.
- The decline is the host's latest act, so `answer_declined` becomes the `cause` even of a run a `resume()` had already ended `failed` or `stopped`.
- `ctx.reason` holds the host's `reason`, and is left out when it gave none. The message doesn't quote it. A `reason` that isn't a `str` or `None` is refused as `invalid_answer`, variant `reason`, with `ctx.got` its class, and the run is left as it was.
- A saved run holds it as it holds a failed call. The next `resume()` calls the node again, so it asks again, under the same id while its inputs and code are the same.
- An id is read by the rules `run.answer` reads it by: one that waits on nothing is `not_waiting`, and one whose place waits with another fingerprint is `answer_stale`.

### Context

The run's context is one object the host passes for a run. It carries what many nodes need but no edge brings, such as the person running the graph or an HTTP client.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Signer:
    name: str


signing = NodeRegistry(context_type=Signer)


@signing.node("sign", title="Sign", description="Signs a text with the name of the person running it.")
def sign(ctx: Context[Signer], text: str) -> str:
    return f"{text}, {ctx.name}"


print(sign(Signer("Ida"), "Done"))  # Done, Ida
signed = Graph.compile(make_graph(sign), signing).run(text="Done", context=Signer("Ida"))
print(signed.outputs)  # {'result': 'Done, Ida'}
```

**Passing it.**

- The host names the context's class once: `NodeRegistry(context_type=X)`.
- It passes the object to every call that starts a run or goes on with one: `graph.run(context=X(...))`, `run.resume(context=...)`, `run.stream(context=...)` and `run.again(context=...)`.
- A run is refused at its start for a context that is not an instance of the class (`invalid_context`). It is refused for no context while a node takes one (`context_missing`, at each such node).
- A graph where no node takes the context runs without one. A context given must still be of the registry's class. A registry that names no class refuses any context (`invalid_context`, variant `no_context_type`).
- The context is never saved with a run, and a call's reuse doesn't look at it (see "Running again").

**Taking it.**

- A node takes the context as its first parameter: `def sign(ctx: Context[X], text: str)`. It is recognised by `Context`, not by the name `ctx`.
- The parameter is no input. No edge reaches it, and no caller fills it in.
- A test calls the node with the context first: `sign(context, "Done")`.
- `Context` anywhere else, such as inside `| None`, in a list or on an output, is `context_misplaced`. And it names a class (`context_not_a_class`).

**What a node may ask for.** A node names the registry's class, a base of it, or a `Protocol` whose members the class has. A `Protocol` is how a node that doesn't know the host's class asks for what it needs. Declare each member of the `Protocol` as a read-only property, since a frozen dataclass doesn't satisfy a plain attribute.

- Compiling checks it. A `Protocol`'s members are checked by name only, and their types are the host's type checker's job.
- A node that asks for what the class is not, or lacks, has `context_does_not_fit` at `(node_id, parameter)`. So does a node that asks for a context on a registry that names none. For a node inside a subgraph, the `loc` goes through the subgraph node.
- `add_subregistry` takes a registry that names the same class, or none. Otherwise it is `context_type_differs`. A registry that names no class refuses a subregistry that names one (`context_type_differs`, variant `on_subregistry_only`).

**Type checking.** `NodeRegistry(context_type=X)` is a `NodeRegistry[X]`. Its graphs are `Graph[X]`, and their runs `Run[X]`. So a type checker refuses a `context=` of another class. It can't see whether a graph's nodes need one.

### Running again

`run.again(**changed)` runs again with some inputs changed and the rest as before. It reuses what it can. A call that would get the same arguments as a call of the same node in the previous run reuses that call's outcome, even if its item moved, and the node isn't called. Answers are reused the same way.

`run.with_inputs(**changed)` is the same run, not started, for `resume()` or `stream()`. It is to `again` what `graph.with_inputs` is to `graph.run`.

```python
@registry.node("send", title="Send", description="Sends a message to a contact.")
def send(contact: str) -> str:
    return f"sent to {contact}"


sending = Graph.compile(make_graph(lines, send), registry)
first = sending.run(text="ida@a.dk\nbo@b.dk")                # two mails
second = first.again(text="ida@a.dk\nbo@b.dk\neva@c.dk")     # one contact added: one mail
```

**What a call is matched by.** The key is what the call is about to receive, by content. To that it adds the node's `@node` id and version, its code (the function's own source as Python parses it, without its name, decorators, comments or docstrings, as a saved run records it, so a new Python version keeps the key; a lambda, or a function with no source file such as one made by `exec`, by its bytecode), its fields, the Series it runs per item of, and whether it may ask (`asks=True`). So a node that stops or starts asking is called again. The run's context is not part of the key.

**Which outcome a call reuses.**

- A call reuses the outcome of the call with the same item indexes, when that call got the same arguments.
- Otherwise it reuses the outcome of any call of the node in the previous run that got the same arguments. So identical items share one previous outcome, and a further identical item reuses it too.

**Answers are taken in order.** A person's answer, or a question still waiting, is taken once, and in item order.

- Of the items that get the same arguments, the first takes the first previous answer and the second the second, whatever thread finished first. An item beyond the answers there were is asked.
- An answer is reused only inside the same outer items. So when documents move, two documents' identical lines keep each document's answers.
- A question still waiting goes on waiting at its item's new place, and nothing new is asked.
- A node that may ask (`asks=True`) has every outcome reused this way, a call that returned without asking too. A node that asks is told apart by its `@node`, not by each call. An item beyond the outcomes there were is called again, and asks only if its function asks.
- A call reused this way waits until it is its turn, and so does everything downstream of it. For example, take `check -> stamp`, both `asks=True`, where `stamp` never asks. `again(items=["zz", "bo"])` reuses nothing of `stamp` for `"bo"` until `check`'s question about `"zz"` is answered, and the run waits.

**Outcomes carried on.** `again` passes on the reusable outcomes the run before it had and didn't use, while their node still has a question waiting. So an answer survives an edit and its revert. Once the node is complete, the unused ones are dropped. So an edit that is undone in the next run calls the node again for the items the edit took out.

**Forgetting.** `run.forget("node", ...)` is a run of the same inputs that calls those nodes again. A subgraph node's id forgets its inner nodes. A node downstream that then gets the same arguments as before is reused. A host checks access again this way.

**Never reuse.** `Policy(reuse_when_inputs_match=False)` is for a node whose result depends on the world, not on its inputs, such as a file read by its path or today's exchange rate. A run made from a previous one (`again`, `with_inputs`, `graph.with_inputs(previous=)`, `forget`) calls it for every item. The policy is checked when that run is made, and again when a saved run is read: `Run.from_json` drops the outcomes a saved run could still reuse for a node whose current `Policy` says `reuse_when_inputs_match=False`, so the rule holds however the run was made.

`node_complete.reused` says how many calls were reused.

### Retries and Timeouts

Retries live on the node's `Policy`, and are counted per call.

- Only an `ExternalError`, or an exception whose class is in `Policy.retry_on`, is retried. An `ExternalError` fails with its own `code`, else `external_failed`; a `retry_on` class fails with `external_failed`.
- Anything else is `execution_failed`, or the node's own `NodeError` code, and runs once.
- A `NodeError` other than `ExternalError`, an `invalid_output` and an `Ask` are never retried, even when `retry_on` names a class they derive from, such as `Exception`.
- Retry `n` waits `retry_delay * 2 ** (n - 1)`, and emits `node_retry`.

**A timeout per attempt.** `Policy.attempt_timeout` limits one attempt. Past it, the call fails with the code `timeout`, and isn't retried. The thread is not interrupted, so the call runs on, and the process waits for it at exit.

**A timeout per resume.** `run.resume(timeout=60)` ends the run `timed_out` when that call of `resume()` takes longer.

- A `timeout` or `checkpoint_every` that is not a finite number of seconds above 0, a `bool` included, is `invalid_limit`, with `ctx.variant` `seconds`, at the call.
- A `max_items` of `True` is `invalid_limit` too.
- Its `ctx.limit` names the limit, and `ctx.value` is the value given.
- Seconds given as another kind of number, such as a `decimal.Decimal`, are read as a `float`.

**Cancelling.** `run.stream(cancel=asyncio.Event())` ends the run `cancelled` when the event is set. A `threading.Event` works too, and a host may also put one in the context for a node to read.

- Leaving the loop once the stream is closed cancels too. But Python closes an async generator left early only when it is collected. So hold it with `async with contextlib.aclosing(run.stream()) as events:`, and loop over `events`.
